Liam to share dedicated capacity pricing and SLA options by 2027-05-11

meeting_header: Date: 2027-05-08 | Time: 16:00 UTC | Duration: 52m | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Neill (Redwood SE), Raj Malhotra (Pegasus VP Eng), Sara Kim (Pegasus SRE), Ethan Lowe (Pegasus CTO)
summary: Postmortem follow-up after Pegasus escalation (2027-04-30). Discussed root cause (KV-cache invalidation + autoscaler interaction), mitigations (rollback, hot-pool warmup, runtime patch), short-term canary plan, and roadmap items for reliability improvements and SLA/contract implications.
topics: Root cause analysis: KV-cache invalidation + autoscaler behavior
transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we know this is follow up to the escalation on April 30th. I sent a short timeline earlier but wanted us to run through it and agree next steps.
[00:20] Raj: thanks Maya, appreciate it. Sara and I will take notes. big impact for us, saw p99 blow up and some token errors in prod during peak.
[00:38] Liam: quick intro from our side, I'm Liam on the infra team, been digging into the runtime traces and kv cache metrics.
[00:47] Ethan: hi all, wanted to make sure we cover what you'll need for a contract-level remediation as well.
[01:05] Sara: quick context: Pegasus runs nightly batch generation and a morning live peak around 09:00 ET. the April 30 incident coincided with a config rollout for a new feature-flag to enable larger sequence processing.
[01:28] Maya: timeline we see: at ~08:55 your traffic ramp hit a burst, autoscaler had recently scaled down a subset of nodes overnight, the new seq feature rolled to 20% traffic at 08:50, and then 08:56 we started seeing increased tail latency and token-generation errors.
[01:55] Raj: correct. our ops page showed spikes in GPU memory churn and some models returned partial completions.
[02:12] Liam: the short version from traces: two things coincided. a bug in our KV cache invalidation logic for large sequence mode caused frequent cache misses on warm KV items, and the cluster autoscaler was aggressively reclaiming a hot pool we rely on to keep KV caches warm. when the warm pool was reclaimed we saw excessive cold-start penalty.
[02:42] Sara: when you say "bug in kv cache invalidation" do you mean eviction logic was too aggressive?
[02:50] Liam: partially. in the large seq codepath the runtime tries to compress the cache and then rehydrate on request. there was a race where the invalidation flag wasn't propagated to all replicas; some nodes kept serving stale pointers, leading to repeated rehydrates. that plus autoscaler squeezing the warm pool meant many requests hit cold state concurrently.
[03:20] Ethan: that maps to the partial completions — the model would time out mid-stream?
[03:26] Liam: yes, streaming connections timed out because the token generation stalled during cache rehydrate, client retried and that amplified load.
[03:36] Raj: we rolled back the seq feature flag at 09:10, is that the recommended immediate action?
[03:44] Maya: yes, rollback was the right short-term mitigation; it reduced load and restored p99 mostly. we also temporarily pinned a subset of your traffic to Redwood Dedicated nodes to stabilize.
[04:00] Sara: can you walk through the pinned/dedicated config? our billing team is worried about cost.
[04:10] Liam: sure — pinned nodes are reserved capacity with a warm-pool configuration so autoscaler won't scale them down under normal reclaim thresholds. we provisioned two pods with reserved GPUs to serve critical routes as an emergency measure. cost impact was moderate but we can run a forecast.
[04:38] Raj: ok understood. next, can you explain root cause in terms we can give to execs?
[04:45] Maya: absolutely: a combination of a cache-management bug in the large-sequence runtime combined with an aggressive autoscaler configuration caused too many requests to experience a cold-start penalty; this led to higher latency and partial outputs. we've prioritized a patch to the runtime and adjustments to autoscaler defaults.
[05:05] Ethan: what is the plan for the runtime patch? timeline?
[05:12] Liam: plan is threefold: 1) hotfix to ensure invalidation flag propagates reliably, 2) introduce a short-lived hot-pool warmup policy so the autoscaler doesn't reclaim warm pools during traffic ramps, 3) add a safer fallback to streaming so timeouts don't cause hard failures. hotfix target is 2027-05-11 for an internal canary, wider rollout 2027-05-18.
[05:45] Sara: sounds good. will you need us to run a reproducer or provide traffic patterns?
[05:52] Liam: yes please — having your traffic replay for the 8k sequence path is ideal. if you can provide a sanitized replay of the April 30 morning window that will help.
[06:05] Raj: we can share a scrubbed trace and traffic histogram. security folks will want assurance on data handling.
[06:12] Maya: we'll accept sanitized artifacts over your secure S3 link or via our secure transfer. note: we have SOC 2 controls and can accept a signed NDA for restricted logs if needed.
[06:27] Ethan: related question: would this be avoided if we moved to Dedicated permanently?
[06:34] Liam: Dedicated reduces the autoscaler variability because you have reserved capacity and warm pools. it doesn't remove the runtime bug, but it reduces the window where cold-start amplification happens. Dedicated + pinning critical routes should strongly mitigate recurrence.
[06:54] Raj: cost/benefit is the discussion; our finance team will need an estimate of monthly reserved cost and expected unit cost reduction from fewer retries.
[07:08] Maya: Liam will share a price/throughput model; we'll also show expected p99 improvements based on canary runs.
[07:18] Sara: what about monitoring — we missed early signals, our incident page only alerted after p95 doubled.
[07:26] Liam: agreed. we propose three monitoring changes: 1) add KV cache miss rate alert with 5m burn rate, 2) add a metric for warm-pool eviction rate, 3) create synthetic load tests that run daily and validate streaming tail latencies for large sequences.
[07:52] Raj: can those be exposed to our dashboard? we use Datadog.
[07:58] Maya: yes, we will push dashboards and alert rules as a Datadog export. we'll also give runbook steps for each alert.
[08:10] Ethan: you mentioned fallback to streaming, does that change semantics? are we risking degraded outputs?
[08:18] Liam: fallback is conservative: if the runtime detects repeated rehydrate stalls it will switch to a safe incremental generation mode that reduces concurrency to avoid timeouts; output quality is slightly slower but avoids partial completions. we think it's acceptable for critical routes.
[08:40] Sara: any risk of regressions from the hotfix? regression testing coverage?
[08:46] Liam: we ran unit and integration tests, but the real risk is in edge traffic shapes. that's why we want to run your replay in the canary cluster before wider rollout. we'll also add specific regression tests to our CI for the large-seq path.
[09:02] Raj: ok timeline recap?
[09:05] Maya: quick recap: logs and scrubbed replay from Pegasus by 2027-05-10, hotfix internal canary 2027-05-11, canary with Pegasus replay by 2027-05-14, wider rollout 2027-05-18, and commercial follow-up on Dedicated pricing by 2027-05-12.
[09:26] Ethan: thanks. can we talk about change control? this was rolled to 20% — would a smaller canary help?
[09:33] Liam: yes, smaller bins and traffic ramping are good practice. we'll also add automatic rollback thresholds tied to kv-miss and p99.
[09:45] Sara: also please include trace ids in alerts so we can cross-reference quickly.
[09:51] Maya: noted. Liam will add trace id exporting to the alert payloads.
[10:00] Raj: any contractual / SLA implications we should discuss now?
[10:06] Maya: short answer: this incident doesn't automatically trigger financial remediation under current usage contract but for larger enterprises we can discuss SLA add-ons for Dedicated. Ethan, you mentioned exec-level needs — we can prepare a customer-facing postmortem doc.
[10:22] Ethan: yes, please. include timeline, RCA, mitigations, and steps to prevent recurrence.
[10:28] Liam: we'll produce an internal postmortem and a sanitized public postmortem for Pegasus execs.
[10:36] Sara: ok, one more ask: can we get a temporary increase in rate limits for the morning window while we test? we need headroom to prevent client retries from tripping limits.
[10:46] Maya: we can provision a temporary quota increase for your account for the morning ramp; we'll coordinate with billing.
[10:54] Raj: thanks. transitioning to technical details — Liam, you said the invalidation flag wasn't propagated; which component owns that message propagation?
[11:04] Liam: the runtime's cache-manager service broadcasts a small invalidation event via our internal pubsub; in the large-seq path a special compression flow bypassed the pubsub notification in some failure branches. it's a logic hole. fix is straightforward but needs careful testing.
[11:26] Ethan: is the pubsub durable? could message loss be a factor?
[11:31] Liam: pubsub is durable but the bypassed branch skipped the ack path, so in a transient error it could fail silently. we'll add stricter ack/wait semantics for invalidation messages.
[11:46] Sara: will this require datastore schema changes?
[11:50] Liam: no schema changes. mostly runtime control flow and some additional telemetry.
[11:56] Raj: good. what's the expected user-visible improvement after hotfix + warm-pool policy? numbers please.
[12:03] Liam: early internal sim suggests p99 should drop from ~1200ms to ~180-220ms on the large-seq path under similar load when warm-pool preserved. error-rate drops to near-zero for partial outputs.
[12:22] Maya: we'll share sim runs and the assumptions.
[12:26] Ethan: on Dedicated, what p99 would you guarantee?
[12:31] Maya: we can propose SLA targets in the pricing doc; typical p99 under Dedicated for these workloads is 200-300ms with our recommended configs. we'll include mitigation commitments in the Dedicated addendum.
[12:49] Raj: ok. earlier you pinned critical routes — will that add coupling? we worry about complexity.
[12:56] Liam: pinning is just an overlay routing rule; it reduces autoscaler interference but is simple to manage. we can template it so you can enable/disable with a single flag.
[13:08] Sara: any feature flags on our side we should change while testing? we have an internal autoscaler tweak we ran last month.
[13:15] Maya: let's exchange config snapshots. Sara send your autoscaler config, we'll send ours, and Liam will highlight differences.
[13:25] Raj: thanks. moving to the incident postmortem deliverable — how will it be structured?
[13:30] Maya: we'll produce: 1) executive summary, 2) timeline, 3) RCA with diagrams, 4) mitigations and short-term actions, 5) long-term roadmap items, 6) impact analysis and QA evidence, 7) CI/regression tests added. expected draft by 2027-05-10.
[13:52] Ethan: good. please mark any customer-facing doc as "sanitized" and share via secure link.
[13:57] Liam: will do.
[14:02] Sara: one ask for reliability improvements: can Redwood add daily synthetic tests that run at our scale? the one-off sims are helpful but daily continuous validation would catch regressions sooner.
[14:12] Maya: agreed. we'll offer synthetic daily runs as part of our Optimize toolkit trial for one month so you can evaluate.
[14:23] Raj: any blockers on the hotfix rollout?
[14:27] Liam: main blocker is reproducer data from you. with a sanitized replay we can run a targeted canary and validate. second blocker is acceptance of temporary quota bump for morning tests.
[14:42] Maya: to close loop: I'll send calendar invites for 05-11 internal canary status and 05-14 canary with Pegasus. I'll also attach the incident timeline, current logs, and the proposed patch diff (sanitized).
[14:56] Raj: thanks. final question: will this affect other customers? any blast radius?
[15:03] Liam: the bug exists in the public runtime and we are proactively rolling fixes; we prioritized customers with large-seq workloads first. low probability for general customers but we will monitor and push patches broadly after internal canaries.
[15:20] Sara: appreciated.
[15:24] Ethan: ok we have what we need.
[15:28] Maya: great—recap of next steps will be in the meeting notes. thanks everyone.
[15:34] Raj: thanks all.
[15:36] Maya: ending call.
